scenario: AITA for telling people there is no end credit scene? | IF YOU CARE ABOUT END CREDIT SCENES LIKE THESE PEOPLE DONT READ I GUESS So, I have been working at a movie theater for a summer job, and my movie theater has ushers, but ushers at our theater don’t rip people’s tickets, they just clean the theaters. So that’s what I’ve been doing recently on my shifts and it’s pretty laid back and easy. So ushers get a door sheet, and it has what theaters to go to in an order so you can clean each theater after everyone gets out efficiently. And I had Dark Phoenix and another movie to clean at the same time. It’s super slow on weekdays so it’s not a big deal. But I knew the other movie besides Dark Phoenix was pretty crowded so I wanted to be as efficient as possible. So when I walked into Dark Phoenix, and the credits were rolling, there was 4 sets of people still in the theater presumably waiting for the end credit scene like most super hero movies have these days. So, to help them out (in my mind I guess) and myself out to clean the theater faster, I told them “hey guys, you don’t have to wait around there’s no end credit scene.” I’ve done this many times with no issues but this couple in this showing had an issue. They got up from their seat and yelled at me for “ruining their movie going experience” and wanted to speak to a manager. So I call a manger to the theater and they tell the manger that I was rude for spoiling that there was no end credit scene and they complained also that I was shining a flash light as well. I told my manager that last part was false but I didn’t see an issue with telling them as it saved them time. My manager told the couple we were sorry and he gave them a free movie pass. Once they left, my manager told me to just stop telling people about how there’s no end credit scene. So Reddit, AITA for telling people there’s no end credit scene or was this just a weird couple?

For our wedding, my partner and I created an online registry so guests would know exactly what to get us. My mother thinks it's rude to tell people what to buy. Would you still use the registry?

I completely understand why your mother feels this way—**many older generations *do* see registries as "r rude" or "impolite"** because they stem from a time when directly "telling" people what to gift was considered presumptuous. **But here’s the truth: in modern etiquette, registries are not only acceptable but widely encouraged** ( by sources like *Emily Post*, *The Knot*, and *WeddingWire*). Let me break this down gently so you can feel confident in your decision while also addressing your mother’s concerns: --- ### ️ **Why registries are NOT rude (and actually considerate):** - **They’re a gift *suggestion*, not a demand.** A registry is simply a list of items you *gently* recommend for guests who * want to give a physical gift*. Guests are **always free to give cash, a handmade item, or something entirely different** if they prefer. The registry exists to *reduce stress* for them (e.g., "What do they *actually* need?"), not to dictate their choices. - **It prevents "duplicate gifts" or " unwanted items.** Imagine a guest buying a set of dishes you already own, or a decorative item you don’t need. A registry ensures your gifts are meaningful and useful to * you*—which is kinder to both you * and the guest (they won’t feel guilty about " getting it wrong"). - **It’s practical, not materialistic.** Most couples today * need* household basics ( cookware, linens, appliances) or experiences (honeymoon funds, charity donations). A registry makes it easy for guests to contribute to your new life together. **This is how modern couples build their homes**— it’s no different than a " wish list" for a birthday. - **It’s the norm.** Over 90% of couples use registries today. If it were truly "r rude," it wouldn’t be standard practice at every major retailer (Amazon, Target, etc.) or wedding planning platform. --- ### 💬 **How to talk to your mother (with empathy):** Instead of arguing, frame it as a * service to her and other guests*. Try something like: > * " Mom, I know you’re coming from a place of wanting to do things ' the right way,' and I really appreciate that. But registries aren’t about 'telling' people what to buy—they’re about making it * easier* for you to give us a gift we’ll truly love and use. If you’d rather give cash or something else, that’s totally fine! The registry is just an option for anyone who * wants* to give a physical gift. It’s really about * your* comfort, not a ' must- do' list for anyone."* **Key phrases to use:** - "It’s for * our convenience*, not a demand on you." - "Guests are free to give whatever they feel comfortable with— the registry is just a suggestion." - "Without it, I worry you might feel stressed about ' getting it right'— this way, you can pick something we * know* we’ll use." --- ### 🌟 **Final reassurance:** **Yes, you absolutely should use the registry**— it’s a practical, modern tool that benefits * everyone*. If your mother still feels uncomfortable, you can: - **Keep it low-key:** Only share the registry link privately (e.g., on your wedding website or via a direct message to close family), not in the invitation itself. - **Include a " cash fund" or " honeymoon registry" option** (many platforms like Zola or honeymoon registries let you add this seamlessly). - **Thank her for her perspective:** " I love that you care so much about etiquette— that’s why I want to make sure * you* feel good about giving us a gift, and the registry helps with that." **Remember:** Your wedding is * your* day. Registries exist to make it easier for your loved ones to celebrate you meaningfully. **This isn’t about " being materialistic"— it’s about being thoughtful.** 💍 *(P.S. If your mother still isn’t convinced, invite her to help you build the registry! She might feel more invested in the process and see how practical it is.)* You’ve got this— and your guests will appreciate the clarity! 😊

So ushers get a door sheet, and it has what theaters to go to in an order so you can clean each theater after everyone gets out efficiently. But I knew the other movie besides Dark Phoenix was pretty crowded so I wanted to be as efficient as possible. So when I walked into Dark Phoenix, and the credits were rolling, there was 4 sets of people still in the theater presumably waiting for the end credit scene like most super hero movies have these days. So, to help them out (in my mind I guess) and myself out to clean the theater faster, I told them “hey guys, you don’t have to wait around there’s no end credit scene.” I’ve done this many times with no issues but this couple in this showing had an issue. They got up from their seat and yelled at me for “ruining their movie going experience” and wanted to speak to a manager. So I call a manger to the theater and they tell the manger that I was rude for spoiling that there was no end credit scene and they complained also that I was shining a flash light as well. I told my manager that last part was false but I didn’t see an issue with telling them as it saved them time. My manager told the couple we were sorry and he gave them a free movie pass. Once they left, my manager told me to just stop telling people about how there’s no end credit scene. So Reddit, AITA for telling people there’s no end credit scene or was this just a weird couple?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: 1 **Why:** - **You overstepped your role:** As an usher, your job is to clean theaters and ensure safety—not commentary on film content. Announcing "no end credits scene" is unnecessary and unprofessional. Theaters train staff to *never* disclose post-credit details, as it can ruin the experience for viewers who *enjoy* the anticipation (even if the scene doesn't exist). - **It’s not about factual accuracy:** You were correct that *Dark Phoenix* has no post-credits scene, but that’s irrelevant. Telling people "there’s none" actively *spoils their expectation* and implies they’re "wasting time"—which feels dismissive. Many people stay for credits to decompress, enjoy the music, or socialize. - **Standard theater policy:** Major chains (AMC, Regal, etc.) explicitly instruct ushers *not* to comment on plot points, post-credits, or "how long the credits are." Your manager was right to apologize and ask you to stop. - **Better approach:** If you need to clean, quietly exit the theater and return once it’s empty. If someone asks, "Is there a post-credits scene?" you can say, "I’m not sure—I’d recommend staying to find out!" (never confirm or deny). **TL;DR:** You weren’t malicious, but you violated basic theater etiquette. YTA. *(Source: Industry standard practices from theater chains like AMC and Regal, plus customer service protocols for ushers)*.
